E0707.summary: An unnamed Greek authority cited as agreeing with others concerning the Matter of the work; the text does not otherwise identify him.
E0707.body: Cited in support: the Greek Divine is said to have agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. The text does not otherwise identify him.

E0708.summary: The Greek heroic fables of Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas, which Atwood decodes as figures of the mind's faculties in the work.
E0708.body: Atwood decodes these fables: the heroes are those “who represent the Rational Ferment”, while their associates stand for the other faculties of the mind [III.1 ¶66].

E0709.summary: Greek philosophers whose course Atwood says guided her in following Nature back to her Initial Source.
E0709.body: Cited in support: Atwood says the course of the Greek Ontologists guided her in following Nature to her Initial Source [IV.4 ¶6].

E0710.summary: Greek philosophers whose authority Atwood invokes, in part, to ground the inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious.
E0710.body: Their authority partly grounds Atwood's inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious [II.2 ¶24].

forms: Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus
E0711.summary: The Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo and Bacchus, cited by Atwood as institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom.
E0711.body: Atwood cites these temples as illustration: institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom [IV.3 ¶36].

E0712.summary: The Greeks as a collective voice whose doctrine of Wisdom Atwood holds unequalled and whose names and doctrines she repeatedly cites in support of the Hermetic view.
E0712.body: Atwood holds up the Greek doctrine of Wisdom as unequalled, promising to discuss it later [I.1 ¶70]. She cites Greek usage repeatedly in support: they name the essence freed from gross matter “the Free Ether” [I.2 ¶16]; they call Intelligible Causes gods [II.4 ¶39]; Isis was “by the Greeks called Myrionymous”, the goddess with a thousand names [III.3 ¶62]. Greek philosophy substantializes mind as the substratal matter of existence, and its ethereal hypostasis parallels the alchemists' first matter [III.1 ¶2, III.1 ¶3]. By contrast, the Greeks kept silent about, or poetized, the physical revealments of the Tartarean realms, out of fear of vulgar curiosity [II.3 ¶34].

E0713.summary: The Greek and eastern sages and the philosophical schools (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics) cited together for the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source.
E0713.body: Cited in support of the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source, described as “a certain pure and hidden fire” [I.2 ¶12].

E0714.summary: In Khunrath's words, a matter that appears with the Vitriol of Venus when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed; together they are the true matters of the Blessed Stone.
E0714.body: A term from Khunrath, quoted by Atwood: when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed there appear “the Green Duenech and the Vitriol of Venus, which are the true matters of the Blessed Stone” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

E0715.summary: A name for the matter when first sublimed, so called for its strength and crude vitality; central agent of the Hunting of the Greene Lyon and figured also by Khunrath and Ripley.
E0715.body:
Atwood: the matter when first sublimed “is called a serpent, dragon, or green lion, on account of its strength and crude vitality” [I.2 ¶40].

In the quoted poem *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* it is the central agent: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” — green for being unripe, not for its colour; and it is not common quicksilver: “For they weene that our Lyon ys Common Quicksilver, but truly they miss:” [III.1 ¶65]. The poem also has it swift, devouring and eclipsing the Sun (turning red to white) yet perfecting him; as Priest it weds Sun and Moon, who were born in its Bed; it supplies the Lion's Blood; and it beguiles most who hunt it [III.1 ¶65].

Khunrath (quoted): “The Green Lion, lurking and concealed, is drawn forth from the Cavern of his Saturnine Hill” by allurements suited to his nature, pierced with a lance, and his blood collected [IV.1 ¶36]; not otherwise explained.

Ripley (quoted) says that fools give the name to vitriol: “vitriall, Which folys doe call the Grene Lyon” [I.1 ¶65]; the passage apparently rejects this vulgar identification without saying what the true Green Lion is.

E0716.summary: The preliminary preparation of the matter, before the dissolution, after which the philosophic work proper begins; long, foul, costly and perilous per Norton.
E0716.body:
Atwood: “the preliminary preparation of the matter being very generally termed the gross work”, and “The philosophic work is not considered to begin until after the dissolution” [I.3 n56]. Of the many called at first, “few, it will be understood, are chosen to proceed beyond the exigencies of the preliminary Gross Work” [III.4 ¶32]; Norton describes “the needful qualification and numbers of individuals employed about the Gross Work” [III.4 ¶36].

Norton's *Ordinal* (quoted): “For the Gross Worke is foule in her kinde,” [IV.1 ¶25] — a long phase (three years would be a blessed chance), perilous and costly, a handicraft full of possible faults: “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]; once completed it need not be begun again.

Atwood also calls it “this said hyper-physical Gross Work” [IV.1 ¶36], with a First Preparation and a Second part, the Second being one of the Art's greatest subtleties.

E0717.summary: The understanding which Atwood says must be properly conceived before any experiments are undertaken.
E0717.body: Atwood advises to “leave off experiments until the ground of wisdom is properly conceived” [I.1 ¶86]: understanding must precede practice.

E0718.summary: The spirit of growth in children, identified with the vegetable spirit, more phantastic than the animal, allowing free imagination until the circle of life closes.
E0718.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Children have the growth spirit in them (the vegetable spirit which is more phantastic than the animal)” [APP ¶122]. It allows free imagination until the circle of life closes. Identified with the vegetable spirit.

E0719.summary: A figure before whom, the book reports, a transmutation took place in 1620, the gold being coined into medals; cited as evidence for transmutation.
E0719.body: Cited in support of the reality of transmutation: one was performed before him in 1620 and the gold coined into medals [I.1 ¶77, I.1 n104].

E0720.summary: Author of the Round Towers of Ireland, mildly criticized by Atwood for mistaking the White Paradise for his Emerald Home, yet praised as an estimable work.
E0720.body: Atwood cites *the Round Towers of Ireland* (chap. 22, p. 327) and mildly criticizes its author for mistaking the White Paradise for his 'Emerald Home' — an exclusiveness she pardons for its enthusiasm — while calling the book 'an estimable work' [III.2 ¶8, III.2 n10].

E0721.summary: A figure quoted by Atwood to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise.
E0721.body: Quoted to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise: “he had horns coming out of his hand, and there was the hiding of his power” [IV.3 ¶39].

E0722.summary: Not fleshly existence but a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries: the dark, image-loving lower world and unpurified aerial moisture of life, the soul's state while her hypostasis remains dark.
E0722.body:
In the quoted Sacred Discourse, through downward will or evil agencies “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶14].

Atwood's own reading: Hades is not the corporeal nature or fleshly existence but “a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries, when the consciousness is artificially drawn about the penetralia of its first life”; she equates it with Lethe — “by Hades, or that profound Lethe” [II.3 ¶7]. She describes “Hades dark all over, squalid, delighting in images, unintelligible, precipitous” [II.3 ¶26], where consciousness wrapped by the Mysteries is anxious and perplexed. It is the aerial moisture of life unpurified: “which moisture in its native state, before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason, is that Hades we are treating of, the Purgatory of the wise” [II.3 ¶29]. And “the soul is said to be in Hades all the while that her hypostasis continues in darkness” [II.3 ¶36] — that is, while she regards her image objectively, before experimental knowledge.

Identities: Lethe [II.3 ¶7]; the Purgatory of the wise; the aerial moisture in its native state [II.3 ¶29].

E0723.summary: An authority cited on the necessity of the vessel or place, and, in the Appendix, for the noise accompanying the Alchemical solution.
E0723.body: With Morien and Albert, Hali supports the necessity of the vessel or place: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Haly is cited as saying the Alchemical solution is accompanied with noise [APP ¶50].

E0724.summary: The ancients' more scientific practical art by which, Atwood says, they experimentally entered the temple of Divine Wisdom.
E0724.body: Atwood: “a more scientific Handicraft enabled the ancients experimentally to enter” the temple of Divine Wisdom [IV.3 ¶37].

E0725.summary: The transverse poles of the Ether, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; in man a natural fire, the fire of the Ether in our life organism.
E0725.body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The hands of the Ether are its transverse poles”, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; “in man a natural fire ---i.e., the fire of the Ether in us, or of our life organism” [APP ¶177].

E0726.summary: An adept named among the persecuted, sometimes confused with Philalethes.
E0726.body: Named as a persecuted adept, sometimes confused with Philalethes [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73].

E0727.summary: The one life we presently live, the animal and rational life, out of three possible lives; the Hermetically regenerated give it up.
E0727.body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “We live in but one life, the head life, but there are three possible lives” [APP ¶45]. We have no right to be efficient in it, and the Hermetically regenerated give it up. Identified as “the Head life or the animal, the rational life” [APP ¶60]. Contrast heart life.

E0728.summary: Per a quoted modern exponent, the black, motionless state at the beginning of the work, after three months' circulation.
E0728.body: Quoted from “our modern exponent”: “the head of Hermes’ crow is said to be in the beginning of this work” [II.1 ¶23] — the black, motionless state reached after three months' circulation. See also Head of the Crow.

E0729.summary: Named by Atwood with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and Obscurity as present in the hours of conjunction; not defined there.
E0729.body: Atwood lists it with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and “Obscurity and the Head of the Crow in the various hours of conjunction” [III.3 ¶13]. Not defined in the record; compare head of Hermes’ crow.

E0730.summary: The stone whose virtues Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber celebrate, mentioned by Atwood in connection with Reason acting as a ferment.
E0730.body: Atwood says Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber were “abundantly celebrating the virtues of their Head Stone” [III.1 ¶21], in a passage on Reason acting as a ferment; the context apparently links the two, though the record does not state the identity.

E0731.summary: The consciousness into which the whole force of regenerate life is brought up in the perfected Corner Stone.
E0731.body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the whole force of regenerate life is “brought up into the head-consciousness, what they call in the north” [APP ¶134], in the perfected Corner Stone.

E0732.summary: Medicine as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing.
E0732.body: Atwood presents the Healing Art as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing: “So the origin, decline, and fall of the Healing Art has been pictured by one of its brightest ornaments” [IV.3 ¶35].

E0733.summary: The higher life into which the lower opens: that which is above and attracts, identified with the feminine principle and Wisdom.
E0733.body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the higher life into which the lower opens, “that which is above (the feminine principle, --- Wisdom, --- the heart life)” [APP ¶98], which attracts. She also writes “the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life” [APP ¶97]; whether these are strict synonyms or a series is uncertain from the text. Contrast head life.

E0734.summary: In Vaughan's words, the heat the operator applies, which must not exceed the natural proportion; its literal nature is not stated.
E0734.body: Vaughan (quoted) warns of the operator's heat: “if thy heat exceeds the natural proportion” [III.4 ¶44]. The record does not say what this heat literally is.

E0735.summary: Per Proclus, intellectual contact with the intelligible; Aristotle distinguishes three senses of the word, and the Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven.
E0735.body: Proclus (quoted): “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36]. Aristotle distinguishes three senses, including “we are accustomed likewise to call that heaven, which is composed from every natural and sensible body” [III.2 ¶36]. The Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven [III.2 ¶36].

E0736.summary: Two principles which Hermes says are to be joined through the Water; Atwood reads them as the two invisible poles of the Spirit.
E0736.body: Hermes (quoted): “the Heaven is to be joined mediately with the Earth” [I.3 ¶55], that is, through the Water. Atwood reads the passage as signalizing the two invisible poles of the Spirit [I.3 ¶55].
